what: Wankel rotary engine kinematics, without combustion. Motor A drives the turntable carrier with a 20-tooth gear on the 28-tooth turntable rim (5:7). The carrier plays the role of the eccentric shaft: it carries the triangular three-apex rotor on an axis 4 mm off-centre. A fixed 16-tooth sun gear, a carried compound idler with two 8-tooth gears and the rotor’s 24-tooth gear make the rotor turn at exactly one third of the carrier speed, in the same direction. The program turns A to 1512° (three carrier turns, one rotor turn) and then back to 0°.
try: Open Apex with its program, press Reset, then Run. Stage 1 confirms the saved datum, stage 2 turns motor A to 1512° at 36°/s (about 42 s), stage 3 returns to 0° at 48°/s.
Follow the rotor centre: it circles the main axis on a 4 mm radius once per carrier turn, three times during stage 2. Meanwhile the rotor itself turns only once.

Pick one apex and follow it: it traces a closed oval with two slight waists, an epitrochoid with the shape of a Wankel housing. All three apexes run along the same curve, a third of a rotor turn apart.

Stop watching the room and look from the carrier: relative to it the rotor turns backwards, two thirds of a turn per carrier turn. After 504° on motor A (one carrier turn) the rotor has turned 120° in the room, so it looks unchanged, but a different apex now leads.
why: Relative to the carrier, the fixed sun gear turns backwards at carrier speed. Through 16 → 8 the idler turns twice as fast, and through 8 → 24 the rotor turns at a third of the idler speed, both meshes reversing direction. So relative to the carrier the rotor turns at −2/3 of the carrier speed, and in the room at ω_c − 2/3·ω_c = ω_c/3. This 3:1 relation is the defining kinematics of the Wankel engine, where an internal gear in the rotor rolls on a fixed pinion with a 3:2 tooth ratio. With the rotor centre e = 4 mm from the axis and the apexes R ≈ 32 mm from the rotor centre, an apex follows x = e·cos 3α + R·cos α, y = e·sin 3α + R·sin α (α = rotor angle): a two-lobed epitrochoid with half-axes R + e ≈ 36 mm and R − e ≈ 28 mm.
matters: A Wankel rotor never stops and reverses like a piston: each of its three faces passes through intake, compression, expansion and exhaust once per rotor turn. That needs the exact 3:1 phase between eccentric shaft and rotor, which this model shows with ordinary spur gears instead of the engine’s internal phasing gear. The model is open: there are no chambers, seals or combustion, so it says nothing about engine torque or efficiency. In a headless run of the Brickwright simulator, 1512.4° measured on the motor shaft gave 1080.3° on the carrier and 360.1° on the rotor (−720.2° relative to the carrier), within 0.002° of the gear ratios at every frame. That is a simulation observation; no physical LEGO build has been tested.
question: Motor A turns 504°. How far has the carrier turned, how far has the rotor turned in the room, and how far relative to the carrier?
answer: Carrier: 504° × 20/28 = 360°, one full turn, so the rotor centre is back where it started. Rotor in the room: 360°/3 = 120°. Relative to the carrier: 120° − 360° = −240°, two thirds of a turn backwards. Because the rotor is a threefold symmetric triangle the pose looks unchanged, but the next apex has taken the place of the first.
further: Sketch the apex path with e = 4 mm and R = 32 mm and compare it with an apex during stage 2. Here R/e = 8; production engines use ratios around 7. A smaller ratio gives a deeper waist.

Count the teeth on the 20-tooth drive, the 28-tooth turntable, the 16-tooth sun, the two 8-tooth idlers and the 24-tooth rotor gear, then check that 1512° on A gives 1080° on the carrier and 360° on the rotor.
The return runs at 48°/s instead of 36°/s. In the ideal gear train the poses are the same in both directions; backlash and friction are not part of that relation.
Compare Cusp Lab, where a rolling gear also draws trochoid curves, and Orbit Mixer, another carrier with gears riding on it.
formula: θ_c = (20/28)·θ_A = (5/7)·θ_A; ω_rotor = ω_c·(1 − (16/8)·(8/24)) = ω_c/3; θ_rotor = (5/21)·θ_A. θ_A = 1512° → θ_c = 1080°, θ_rotor = 360°. Apex path (rotor angle α): x = e·cos 3α + R·cos α, y = e·sin 3α + R·sin α, with e ≈ 4 mm (10 LDU) and R ≈ 32 mm (80 LDU), read from the model geometry.
